issue_context.title: journalctl -F shows the same values multiple times
issue_context.body:
I think this doesn't make any sense... We should return just a list of unique items.

```console
$ journalctl -F _TRANSPORT|sort|uniq -c|sort -g
     17 driver
     39 audit
     39 kernel
     67 stdout
     70 syslog
     95 journal
```

systemd 248-106-g3e23a7b
comments:
That looks like a bug to me, the code makes an effort to not return duplicates from multiple journals @ https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/v248/src/libsystemd/sd-journal/sd-journal.c#L2967

afraid I don't have time to dig deeper into this anytime soon, bisect?

review_comments:
uh this is weird, why is the compiler complaining about these:

```
../src/libsystemd/sd-journal/sd-journal.c: In function â€˜sd_journal_get_cutoff_monotonic_usecâ€™:
../src/libsystemd/sd-journal/sd-journal.c:2838:25: error: â€˜toâ€™ may be used uninitialized in this function [-Werror=maybe-uninitialized]
 2838 |                 *ret_to = to;
      |                 ~~~~~~~~^~~~
../src/libsystemd/sd-journal/sd-journal.c:2836:27: error: â€˜fromâ€™ may be used uninitialized in this function [-Werror=maybe-uninitialized]
 2836 |                 *ret_from = from;
      |                 ~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~
```

They are return values? Wut?
Ah no, I misread and thought it was complaining that the variables were unused. I should probably go to sleep.
It's angry because `ORDERED_HASHMAP_FOREACH` might never enter the block of code assigning to/from.
aye, I had read it as `-Wunused-variable`

The logic is slightly different here now right? Before, if the return values `*from`/`*to` were set, they could potentially have overshadowed any `fr`/`t` found while iterating on the hashmap (ie: if `*from` was smaller than all the values found in the iteration, it would have been returned unchanged). Now they will be ignored. Was the previous behavior intentional, and is the change intentional too?

Actually in the old code we'd override what's in the return parameters if at least one file was found (that's because `found` is initially false, in which case we'll override whatever is written into these values). If no file was found we'd leave the values untouched, but still succeed. And that is really a bug: we should initialized all return params on sucess and leave them untouched on failure, as per coding style. Thus, with the new code we follow the coding style here, as when we don#t have any file open we'll now reset the return parameters to UINT64_MAX.
Ah yes of course, missed that there's the first iteration special casing, thanks
